title: Serving: Decoding and the KV Cache
oneLiner: A model only gives probabilities for the next word; decoding rules choose the word, and a memory of past keys and values (the KV cache) makes each new word fast, but costs a lot of memory.

what.html:
When a model answers, it first reads your whole prompt at once (prefill), then writes the reply one token at a time (decode). At each step it produces a probability for every possible next token, and a decoding rule picks one: always the top choice (greedy), the best few sentences (beam search), or a random draw from the likely ones (top-k, top-p, temperature). To avoid redoing work, it keeps the keys and values of past tokens in a KV cache.

Everyday versionWriting a story with a friend who suggests next words with odds. You can always take their favourite, keep a few drafts going, or roll dice among the sensible ones. Your notes on what has been written so far are the cache: you don't reread the whole story each time.

why.html:
• The decoding rule changes whether answers are precise, varied or repetitive.
  • Speed per word is limited by memory reading, which shapes cost.
  • The KV cache decides how many users and how much context fit on a GPU.

how.title: Read the prompt, then write
how.html: Prefill handles the whole prompt in one go and fills the cache. Decode then adds one token per step, reusing everything cached.

how.title: Greedy or beam
how.html: Greedy takes the top word each time and can paint itself into a corner. Beam search keeps a few candidate sentences and can find a better overall one.

how.title: Top-k: a shortlist of k
how.html: Keep the k most likely words and pick randomly among them, weighted by their odds. Simple, but k doesn't adapt to how sure the model is.

how.title: Top-p: a shortlist that adapts
how.html: Keep just enough words to cover p of the probability. With (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10) and p = 0.9, the first three stay and the last is dropped.

how.title: Temperature: a creativity dial
how.html: Low temperature makes the favourite even more likely; high temperature spreads the chances out. Near zero it behaves like greedy.

how.title: Reading memory is the slow part
how.html: Each new word means reading every weight once. A 7B model (14 GB) on a 2 TB/s GPU can't go faster than about 143 words per second for one user.

how.title: How big is the cache?
how.html: About half a megabyte per token for a 32-layer model: 2,048 tokens take 1 GB. Many users with long chats can need more memory than the model itself.

how.title: Share the keys and values
how.html: Let groups of attention heads share one set of keys and values (GQA, MQA), or store a compressed summary (MLA). The cache shrinks 4× to 32×.

demo.html: Pick the decoding setting that fits each job.

example.html:
Cache arithmetic. 2 (key and value) × 32 layers × 4,096 numbers × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes per token. Multiply by 2,048 tokens: about 1 GB for a single conversation.

Supplementary Repetition penalties lower the scores of words already used, which helps stop sampled text from looping.

misunderstandings: Greedy decoding gives the most likely sentence.
Only the most likely next word each step.
Deterministic, but can be dull or loop.
Decoding speed depends mainly on GPU compute.
The KV cache is small next to the model.
With long contexts and many users it can exceed the weights.
takeaways: Prefill is parallel and compute-bound; decode is one token at a time and bandwidth-bound.
Greedy is myopic; beam search keeps B candidates.
Top-k uses a fixed shortlist; top-p adapts (p = 0.9 keeps 3 of 0.5/0.25/0.15/0.10).
KV cache = 2·L·d·bytes per token (0.5 MiB for 32 × 4096 × 16-bit); GQA/MQA/MLA shrink it.
thirty: Generation runs a compute-bound prefill over the prompt (filling the KV cache; sets time to first token) and a bandwidth-bound decode loop, one token per step, reusing cached keys and values. Decoding rules: greedy (argmax, myopic), beam search (keep B best sequences; good for translation, bland for open text), top-k (sample among k most likely), top-p (smallest set reaching cumulative p; p = 0.9 on 0.5/0.25/0.15/0.10 keeps 3), and temperature (logits/T; low sharpens, high flattens). Each decode step reads all weights for ~2 FLOPs per parameter, so speed is limited by memory bandwidth: 7B × 2 B = 14 GB at 2 TB/s → 7 ms/token. The KV cache costs 2·L·d·bytes per token (524,288 B for 32 layers × 4096 × 16-bit; 1 GiB per 2048 tokens) and grows with context and users. MQA (one shared K/V head), GQA (groups share) and MLA (compressed latent) cut it 4–32×.
